headline: Sudan: More than half of children assessed in Jebel Marra stunted as drought worsens hunger crisis
snippet: KHARTOUM, 28 October 2026 – More than half of children assessed in Jebel Marra, one of Sudan's most isolated and food-insecure regions, are chronically malnourished, according to new Save the Children data, highlighting the growing impact of conflict and the El-Niño weather event. New data from Save the Children in Central Jebal Marra found 57% of children are chronically malnourished (known as stunted) while 15% of children assessed – or nearly one in six - were acutely malnourished [1]. Stunting, meaning a child has low height for their age, reflects chronic or recurrent undernutrition while acute malnutrition or wasting, meaning a child has low weight for their height due to recent or ongoing severe weight loss or failure to gain weight. Both forms of malnutrition can have lasting consequences for children's health and development. As a result of conflict, food shortages, limited access to healthcare, clean water and sanitation, the survey found that over four in 10 (43%) children in Central Jebel Marra had been ill in the two weeks preceding the survey. A total of 69% of households surveyed relied on unsafe or untreated water. The findings underline the urgent need for an integrated response to malnutrition that addresses not only children's immediate nutritional needs, but also access to food, healthcare, safe water, sanitation and protection from diseases, said Save the Children. Jebel Marra, a usually fertile and food producing area of Sudan, is being hit by the combined effects of conflict, severe drought, disrupted livelihoods and a critically underfunded humanitarian response. Lack of rainfall has also led to shortages of animal fodder, placing further pressure on herders. Global hunger monitor, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), last week warned that conflict, displacement and severe El Niño-induced drought are increasing the risk of famine in parts of Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan. The ongoing conflict in Sudan has caused the world’s largest displacement crisis, forcing about 11 million people from their homes, with at least 19 million people – or two in every five Sudanese – facing acute food insecurity, according to the World Food Programme. The impact of drought and Sudan’s wider hunger crisis is also being felt beyond Darfur. In Gedaref, seven-month-old Hamza* lost his mother shortly after birth and was cared for by his grandmother, Khadija*. When he became seriously ill, she took him to a Save the Children-supported stabilisation centre, where he was diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition and received treatment. He is now recovering. “When we arrived at the stabilisation centre, the doctors and nurses immediately began treating him,” said Khadija. “Today, he smiles, plays and looks like a different child.” Claire Henery, Country Director for Save the Children in Sudan, said: “Children in Sudan are being hit by crisis upon crisis. Conflict has already devastated livelihoods and access to essential services, and drought is deepening an already severe crisis. “ Our latest findings from Central Jebel Marra show children facing both acute malnutrition and the long-term effects of inadequate nutrition. At the same time, many families lack safe water, and children remain vulnerable to disease. “The international community cannot look away. We urgently need a large-scale integrated response and sustained access to provide food security, life-saving nutrition, healthcare and clean water while strengthening the systems children depend on.” Save the Children has worked in Sudan since 1983 and provides programming for children and families affected by conflict, displacement, extreme poverty and hunger. Save the Children has recently launched a $300 million global humanitarian nutrition initiative for 2026–2028 bringing together public and private funders to treat and prevent child malnutrition and illness in the toughest humanitarian contexts – including in Sudan. Partners joining this initiative are helping reshape the future of humanitarian nutrition, redesigning the way the world treats malnutrition – from a reactive system focused on treating crisis to one that prevents it. headline: CIA - Black Tie Optional - Review : Down To Party
snippet: I think this episode of CIA has been my favourite of the whole show so far. I loved every single aspect of it but most of all, I loved being able to see Bill and Colin really lean on each other and know that they can trust each other when put in serious situations. Episode one Colin and Bill would not have been able to cohesively deal with the undercover op going wrong and it’s so fun to see where they are now. One of the best things they have done that has bled from the first season is having an overarching storyline. I enjoyed the mole storyline last year but I’m definitely more interested in what happened with Bill’s dad and Felix Vincent. It ties everything together so well. The past couple episodes, Colin has seemed very in touch with his emotions and it’s been so great to watch. Even if he does use jokes to get through his feelings, it’s wonderful to see a stoic man’s emotions portrayed on screen. Bill is also really going through it this season, I did like him questioning if he should really be looking into his dad’s past or not. I do think there is a level of grief that he is looking into his dad because he’s no longer alive. The set up for Bill’s father’s watch was so good, normally I see it coming but when Colin found the chip it made all the more sense why it was mentioned that Bill had it at the start of the episode. The suspense of what Bill’s dad was doing and why Felix went rogue makes sure that I am tuning in each episode. I can’t wait to see what they uncover next!

headline: From golden population to golden workforce: The human side of Vietnam's AI vision
snippet: Dr Tan Hong Ming, Assistant Dean (Digital Operations), NUS Business School (sixth from left), with Ms Tara Bal, Head of Corporate Communications, NUS Business School (fifth from right), together with representatives from the Vietnamese media. HANOI, VIETNAM - Media OutReach Newswire - 27 October 2026 - As Vietnam pursues its ambition of becoming a high-income developed economy by 2045, artificial intelligence (AI) is expected to play a growing role in supporting productivity and innovation. Alongside technology adoption, developing the skills and management capabilities to apply AI effectively is becoming an important part of the country's workforce agenda. A 2026 study commissioned by Amazon Web Services (AWS) found that 26 per cent of Vietnamese businesses have adopted AI, up from 18 per cent a year earlier. However, 61 per cent of adopters remain at the experimentation stage, while 87 per cent of surveyed employers consider reskilling existing employees important to their AI strategies. Vietnam has also prioritised workforce development through its national AI human resources development programme, approved in August 2026. The programme includes plans to equip around 10 million workers with basic AI skills by 2030, alongside developing specialised AI talent and strengthening AI education. Dr Tan Hong Ming, Assistant Dean (Digital Operations) at the National University of Singapore (NUS) Business School, said workforce development needs to extend beyond technical proficiency. "AI literacy is only the starting point. The bigger challenge is whether organisations know how to redesign work around AI. A company can train every employee to use AI tools and still see little improvement in productivity if its processes and management practices remain unchanged. This is why leadership capability matters just as much as technical skills," said Dr Tan at a media engagement session in Hanoi. From adopting AI to creating business value As AI tools become more accessible, businesses face decisions about where the technology can be applied, how existing work processes may need to change and what employees need to learn. Dr Tan believes that while AI can improve productivity by automating tasks, organisations must also consider how its growing use affects the way employees learn and develop expertise. "Struggle is an important part of learning. We develop expertise and judgement by working through difficult problems, making mistakes and figuring things out for ourselves. AI can now take away much of that struggle by providing answers almost instantly. While this improves productivity, we need to be careful that we are not also removing the experiences that help people learn and grow. Organisations need to rethink how employees develop these capabilities in an AI-enabled workplace," he said. Beyond developing AI literacy, organisations need to consider how employees assess AI-generated information, how managers incorporate the technology into workflows and how senior leaders oversee its use in business decisions. Rethinking how professionals learn The growing use of AI also raises questions about how professionals acquire the experience and judgement needed to take on more complex responsibilities. While AI can help generate information and recommendations, learning to make business decisions still requires opportunities to question assumptions, evaluate competing perspectives and work through problems without complete information. NUS Business School is piloting an AI-enabled business simulation that allows MBA and Executive MBA students to practise these capabilities. The simulation uses ScholAIstic, a generative AI platform developed by the NUS AI Centre for Educational Technologies (AICET). Dr Emir Hrnjić, Senior Lecturer in Finance at NUS Business School, has been working with AICET to adapt and refine the platform's capabilities for management education, creating AI-simulated executives whom students interview before making business recommendations. Professor Teo Chung Piaw, Dean of NUS Business School, said the growing capabilities of AI require business schools to examine not only what students learn, but also how they develop and apply their knowledge. "The role of business education is changing as AI becomes part of how organisations operate and make decisions. We cannot simply introduce new technology into existing teaching methods and assume that learning will improve. Business schools need to examine what students should learn, how they acquire that knowledge and how their ability to apply it is assessed. Our approach is to use AI to create more opportunities for students to think critically, engage with different perspectives and exercise independent judgement," said Prof Teo. Beyond preparing graduates for the workplace, postgraduate programmes and Executive Education can provide opportunities for working professionals and senior executives to update their knowledge and develop the capabilities needed to manage technological and organisational change. Building Vietnam's golden workforce Vietnam's Vision 2045 places continued emphasis on productivity, innovation and the development of higher-value industries. As AI becomes more widely adopted, higher education and professional training can contribute by equipping graduates, managers and senior executives with the capabilities to apply technology effectively in business. Dr Tan said the country's demographic advantage provides a foundation for developing these capabilities throughout people's careers. "Vietnam's demographic advantage gives it an important opportunity, but a young workforce alone does not guarantee economic success. The real opportunity is to develop a workforce that can continuously learn, adapt and create value alongside AI. If Vietnam can combine its human capital with the effective adoption of AI, it can turn its golden population into a golden workforce," he said. The school has consistently ranked first in Asia by independent publications and agencies, such as The Financial Times and Quacquarelli Symonds, in recognition of the quality of its programmes, faculty research and graduates.
